title: LLM Evaluation & Testing
blurb: Evaluation as its own engineering discipline -- golden datasets, metric selection, LLM-as-judge auditing, human/pairwise evaluation, RAG/agent evaluation, and continuous regression testing.

description: Golden datasets, metric selection, LLM-as-judge auditing, human and pairwise evaluation, RAG/agent evaluation, and regression testing -- the shared methodology existing courses only touch narrowly.

lessons.title: Evaluation Is an Engineering Discipline
objectives: Explain why evaluation is evidence for a specific claim, not a demo of selected examples
Explain how evaluation as evidence changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect evaluation as evidence with system vs. model quality and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A handful of impressive demo examples proves the system can work, not that it does work reliably.
examples:
# system quality vs. model quality -- genuinely different claims:
# model quality: 'this LLM scores well on a general public benchmark'
# system quality: 'THIS specific feature, built on that model, reliably helps
# users complete THEIR actual task' -- a strong underlying model does not
# automatically mean the system built on top of it is actually good
commonMistakes: Showing a handful of impressive demo examples as if that constitutes evaluation -- a demo proves the system CAN work in that case; it says nothing about how often it works across the real.
lessons.careerRelevance: Every other lesson in this course builds on treating evaluation as evidence for a claim -- this framing is what separates real evaluation engineering from selecting flattering examples.
lessons.explain: A handful of impressive demo examples proves the system can work, not that it does work reliably.

# model quality: 'this LLM scores well on a general public benchmark'
# system quality: 'THIS specific feature, built on that model, reliably helps
# users complete THEIR actual task' -- a strong underlying model does not
# automatically mean the system built on top of it is actually good

lessons.title: Defining Goals and Success Criteria
objectives: Convert a vague goal into testable acceptance criteria and identify failure categories
Explain how testable success criteria changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect testable success criteria with hard constraints vs. optimization goals and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A goal like 'make the assistant better' or 'more accurate' isn't yet testable -- it must be converted into specific, checkable criteria: what does 'better' mean for THIS feature, what's the primary objective versus secondary ones, what are the hard constraints (must never do X) versus optimization goals (should generally do more of Y).
examples:
# converting a vague goal into testable criteria:
# vague: 'make the assistant more accurate'
# testable: 'the assistant must never fabricate a specific dollar amount
# (hard constraint); it should correctly resolve at least 90% of billing
# questions without escalation (optimization goal); failure categories include
# wrong amount, wrong policy citation, and unnecessary escalation'
commonMistakes: Leaving a goal vague ('more accurate,' 'more helpful') without converting it into specific, checkable criteria -- an untestable goal can't actually be evaluated, only vaguely gestured at.
lessons.careerRelevance: Converting a vague product ask into testable criteria is exactly the first, most consequential step of any real evaluation project.
lessons.explain: A goal like 'make the assistant better' or 'more accurate' isn't yet testable -- it must be converted into specific, checkable criteria: what does 'better' mean for THIS feature, what's the primary objective versus secondary ones, what are the hard constraints (must never do X) versus optimization goals (should generally do more of Y).

# converting a vague goal into testable criteria:
# vague: 'make the assistant more accurate'
# testable: 'the assistant must never fabricate a specific dollar amount

# questions without escalation (optimization goal); failure categories include
# wrong amount, wrong policy citation, and unnecessary escalation'

lessons.title: Offline and Online Evaluation
objectives: Distinguish offline from online evaluation and explain why their results can genuinely differ
Explain how offline evaluation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect offline evaluation with online evaluation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Offline evaluation runs against a fixed dataset before deployment -- controlled and repeatable, but it can't fully capture real user behavior. Online evaluation observes real production traffic -- user feedback, A/B testing, and canary evaluation conceptually compare real outcomes, but labels may be immediate, delayed, or sometimes never available at all.
examples:
# why offline success does not guarantee online success:
# offline: 'candidate scores 92% on our fixed golden dataset' -- controlled,
# repeatable, but the dataset can't capture every real user request pattern
# online: real users ask things the offline dataset never anticipated --
# offline and online evaluation answer genuinely DIFFERENT questions
commonMistakes: Treating a strong offline evaluation result as proof the system will perform well in production -- offline and online evaluation answer different questions, and real user behavior can.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding this gap (not just running an offline benchmark once) is exactly what distinguishes evaluation engineering from a one-time academic exercise.
lessons.explain: Offline evaluation runs against a fixed dataset before deployment -- controlled and repeatable, but it can't fully capture real user behavior. Online evaluation observes real production traffic -- user feedback, A/B testing, and canary evaluation conceptually compare real outcomes, but labels may be immediate, delayed, or sometimes never available at all.

lessons.title: Golden Datasets and Representative Test Cases
objectives: Build a golden dataset that genuinely represents real usage, correctly versioned and separated from development data
Explain how golden datasets changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect golden datasets with representative sampling and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A golden (reference) dataset is a curated, documented set of cases with either an expected output or clear acceptable-output criteria -- built from a representative mix of real and synthetic cases, not just whatever was convenient to collect.
examples:
# a real, subtle risk: accidental reuse of development examples
# during prompt iteration, a developer repeatedly checks the system against
# the SAME 10 examples until they look good -- then uses those same 10
# examples as the 'evaluation set' -- this doesn't measure real generalization,
# it measures fit to exactly the cases already optimized against
commonMistakes: Accidentally using the same examples for both prompt/system iteration and final evaluation -- this inflates apparent performance without measuring genuine generalization to new, unseen.
lessons.careerRelevance: A well-documented, versioned golden dataset is one of the most durable, reusable artifacts an evaluation engineer produces.

lessons.title: Adversarial, Edge-Case and Slice-Based Evaluation
objectives: Explain why aggregate scores can hide important regressions, and how slice-based evaluation surfaces them
Explain how aggregate-score masking changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect aggregate-score masking with slice-based evaluation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A strong aggregate score can hide a real, important failure -- if 95% of your evaluation set is easy, routine cases, a system that fails badly on the remaining 5% (which might be your highest-stakes cases) can still show an impressive-looking overall number.
examples:
# how an aggregate score can hide a real regression:
# 95% easy cases pass perfectly, 5% hard/critical cases fail completely
# aggregate score: 95% -- looks excellent
# per-slice score: 100% (easy), 0% (critical) -- reveals the actual, serious problem
# an aggregate-only report would have completely missed this
commonMistakes: Reporting only an aggregate score without breaking results down by slice -- a strong overall number can hide a complete failure in a smaller, possibly higher-stakes subset of cases.
lessons.careerRelevance: Slice-based evaluation is exactly what separates a genuinely rigorous evaluation report from a single reassuring-looking number.

lessons.title: Deterministic and Rule-Based Metrics
objectives: Apply deterministic metrics appropriately, and recognize their limits for open-ended output
Explain how exact match changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect exact match with schema/rule-based validation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Deterministic metrics give a clear, reproducible pass/fail: exact match, normalized exact match (ignoring case/whitespace differences), regex or rule-based checks, JSON/schema validity, required-field presence, and action/tool-call validity against an allowlist.
examples:
# where deterministic metrics genuinely work, and where they don't:
# 'is this valid JSON matching our schema?' -> deterministic check works perfectly
# 'is this a good, helpful explanation of a concept?' -> no deterministic check
# can capture this; the output is open-ended, with no single correct string
commonMistakes: Applying an exact-match check to open-ended, free-form output -- a correct paraphrase or equally valid alternative phrasing will fail this check despite being a genuinely good answer.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing precisely which tasks deterministic metrics fit (and which they don't) is foundational before reaching for a subjective or model-based metric instead.
lessons.explain: Deterministic metrics give a clear, reproducible pass/fail: exact match, normalized exact match (ignoring case/whitespace differences), regex or rule-based checks, JSON/schema validity, required-field presence, and action/tool-call validity against an allowlist.

lessons.title: Semantic and Model-Based Similarity Metrics
objectives: Explain why semantic similarity to a reference answer does not guarantee factual correctness
Explain how semantic/embedding-based similarity changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect semantic/embedding-based similarity with reference-answer dependence and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Semantic similarity (often computed via embedding-based comparison) measures how close a response is in MEANING to a reference answer, capturing valid paraphrases that exact match would incorrectly reject.
examples:
# why HIGH semantic similarity does not prove factual correctness:
# reference: 'the return window is 30 days'
# candidate: 'the return window is 90 days' -- HIGH semantic similarity
# (same topic, same sentence structure, same general meaning) but factually
# WRONG -- semantic similarity measures closeness in MEANING, not truth
commonMistakes: Treating a high semantic-similarity score as proof of factual correctness -- a response can be very close in overall meaning to a reference while still stating a specific wrong fact.
lessons.careerRelevance: This exact gap (semantic closeness vs. factual truth) is why evaluation systems combine semantic metrics with dedicated factuality checks, covered later in this course.
lessons.explain: Semantic similarity (often computed via embedding-based comparison) measures how close a response is in MEANING to a reference answer, capturing valid paraphrases that exact match would incorrectly reject.

lessons.title: LLM-as-a-Judge and Its Failure Modes
objectives: Name specific, documented failure modes of automated LLM judging, and explain why judges must be audited, not trusted by default
Explain how LLM-as-a-judge changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect LLM-as-a-judge with answer-order sensitivity and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: LLM-as-a-judge uses a model to grade another model's output against a rubric -- reference-based (comparing to a known-good answer) or reference-free, pointwise (scoring one response) or pairwise (comparing two).
examples:
# a judge's number is not automatically ground truth -- it's a measurement
# subject to its own design flaws:
# answer-order sensitivity: swap which answer is shown first -> the judge's
# preference can flip, even though nothing about the ANSWERS changed
# verbosity preference: a longer, padded, factually worse answer can be
# preferred over a shorter, correct one -- length itself biasing the grade
commonMistakes: Treating an automated judge's score as objective ground truth simply because it's produced by a model and expressed as a number -- judges have documented, real biases (order, verbosity.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding and being able to name these specific judge failure modes (not just 'LLM judges can be biased' vaguely) is a genuine, distinguishing depth in real evaluation engineering roles.
lessons.explain: LLM-as-a-judge uses a model to grade another model's output against a rubric -- reference-based (comparing to a known-good answer) or reference-free, pointwise (scoring one response) or pairwise (comparing two).

# preferred over a shorter, correct one -- length itself biasing the grade

lessons.title: Pairwise Comparison and Ranking
objectives: Design a counterbalanced pairwise comparison protocol and interpret win rates with appropriate uncertainty
Explain how pairwise comparison changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pairwise comparison with counterbalanced ordering and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pairwise comparison (is response A or response B better, for the same input) is often genuinely easier and more reliable than absolute scoring, since humans and judges are typically better at relative comparison than assigning a stable absolute number.
examples:
# why counterbalancing order matters for pairwise comparison:
# without counterbalancing: A is ALWAYS shown first -- if there's any position
# bias at all, it's now indistinguishable from A actually being better
# with counterbalancing: A first for half the comparisons, B first for the
# other half -- position bias, if present, cancels out rather than contaminating the result
commonMistakes: Running pairwise comparisons without counterbalancing presentation order -- any position bias present becomes indistinguishable from a genuine quality difference between A and B.
lessons.careerRelevance: Pairwise comparison protocols (with proper counterbalancing) are the standard, real-world method behind most production model/prompt comparison decisions.

Connect rubric design with scoring anchors and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: Human evaluation remains essential for genuinely subjective qualities automated metrics can't fully capture. A good rubric has clear scoring anchors (concrete examples of what a 3 vs.
examples:
# what makes a rubric ANCHOR concrete, not just a numeric scale:
# vague: 'rate helpfulness from 1 to 5'
# anchored: '5 = fully resolves the question with accurate, complete detail;
# 3 = partially helpful but missing key information; 1 = unhelpful or
# actively misleading' -- with a WORKED EXAMPLE for each anchor point
commonMistakes: Using a numeric rating scale with no concrete anchors or examples -- different reviewers will interpret '3 out of 5' completely differently without shared, concrete reference points for what.
lessons.careerRelevance: A well-anchored rubric is what makes human evaluation actually reproducible across different reviewers, rather than each reviewer effectively grading on their own private scale.

lessons.title: Factuality, Hallucination and Groundedness Evaluation
objectives: Precisely distinguish factual correctness, faithfulness, groundedness, and citation correctness
Explain how factual correctness changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect factual correctness with faithfulness and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: These related-sounding terms mean genuinely different things: factual correctness asks whether a claim is true in the world; faithfulness to provided context asks whether the response accurately reflects what was actually given to the model (even if that source material itself were wrong).
examples:
# distinct failure modes, easy to conflate:
# faithful to context but factually wrong: the source document itself was
# outdated, and the response accurately reflects that outdated document
# groundedness failure: the response states something the context never said
# at all -- fluent, plausible-sounding, but simply invented
# citation failure: cites a real source, but that source doesn't actually say what's claimed
commonMistakes: Treating a fluent, confident, relevant-sounding response as evidence it's factually correct -- fluency and relevance are properties of the TEXT; factual support is a separate question.
lessons.careerRelevance: Precisely distinguishing these terms (not using them interchangeably) is exactly the vocabulary real evaluation engineering and factuality research is built on.
lessons.explain: These related-sounding terms mean genuinely different things: factual correctness asks whether a claim is true in the world; faithfulness to provided context asks whether the response accurately reflects what was actually given to the model (even if that source material itself were wrong).

lessons.title: Evaluating RAG Systems
objectives: Separate retrieval evaluation from generation evaluation to correctly attribute a RAG failure
Explain how retrieval vs. generation failure changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect retrieval vs. generation failure with recall-oriented retrieval checks and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A bad RAG answer can fail for two genuinely different reasons: retrieval failure (the system didn't find the relevant document at all) or generation failure (it found the right document but the model still produced a wrong or ungrounded answer from it) -- and the fix for each is completely different.
examples:
# why attribution matters -- the SAME bad answer, two different real causes:
# cause 1 (retrieval failure): the relevant document was never retrieved at all
# -- fixing this means improving the retrieval step (indexing, query, ranking)
# cause 2 (generation failure): the relevant document WAS retrieved correctly,
# but the model still produced an ungrounded or wrong answer from it --
# fixing THIS means improving prompting/generation, not retrieval at all
commonMistakes: Treating every bad RAG answer as a generation problem (or every one as a retrieval problem) without checking which stage actually failed -- misattributing the failure means fixing the wrong.
lessons.careerRelevance: This retrieval-vs-generation attribution is one of the most practically useful, frequently-tested skills in real RAG system debugging and evaluation.
lessons.explain: A bad RAG answer can fail for two genuinely different reasons: retrieval failure (the system didn't find the relevant document at all) or generation failure (it found the right document but the model still produced a wrong or ungrounded answer from it) -- and the fix for each is completely different.

# cause 2 (generation failure): the relevant document WAS retrieved correctly,

# fixing THIS means improving prompting/generation, not retrieval at all

lessons.title: Evaluating Agents, Tools and Safety-Critical Behavior
objectives: Evaluate an agent's actions and tool effects, not merely its final natural-language answer
Explain how tool selection/argument evaluation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tool selection/argument evaluation with sequence correctness and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An agent can produce a perfectly reasonable-sounding final answer while having taken genuinely wrong or dangerous actions along the way -- evaluating only the final text misses this entirely.
examples:
# why evaluating only the final answer misses real agent failures:
# final answer: 'I've updated your shipping address as requested' -- sounds
# completely fine and reasonable
# actual side effect: the agent updated the WRONG customer's record, or called
# an unauthorized action along the way -- none of this shows up if you only
# evaluate the final natural-language text, not the actual actions taken
commonMistakes: Evaluating an agent only by reading its final natural-language answer -- this misses tool-selection errors, wrong arguments, unauthorized side effects, and failed recovery, all of which can.
lessons.careerRelevance: This action-and-side-effect-focused evaluation is exactly what separates genuine agent evaluation from simply grading a chatbot's final message.

lessons.title: Prompt, Model and Pipeline Regression Testing
objectives: Design a regression test comparing baseline vs. candidate that cannot hide a critical-slice regression behind an improved aggregate score
Explain how baseline vs. candidate changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect baseline vs. candidate with per-slice regression and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Any change -- a new prompt version, a new model version, a retrieval index update -- needs regression testing against a versioned evaluation dataset: comparing a baseline's results to a candidate's, per overall score AND per slice, since (as covered earlier) an aggregate improvement can hide a critical-slice regression that would otherwise go unnoticed.
examples:
# why per-slice regression testing matters, restated concretely here:
# baseline overall: 80% | candidate overall: 83% -- looks like a clear improvement
# baseline security slice: 85% | candidate security slice: 60% -- a SEVERE
# regression, completely hidden by the improved aggregate number -- exactly
# the kind of result a regression test must be designed to catch, not miss
commonMistakes: Approving a candidate based only on an improved aggregate score, without checking per-slice results for a hidden regression -- an aggregate improvement can mask a serious regression in a.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is exactly the discipline that prevents a well-intentioned prompt or model update from silently shipping a serious regression in production.
lessons.explain: Any change -- a new prompt version, a new model version, a retrieval index update -- needs regression testing against a versioned evaluation dataset: comparing a baseline's results to a candidate's, per overall score AND per slice, since (as covered earlier) an aggregate improvement can hide a critical-slice regression that would otherwise go unnoticed.
lessons.example:
# why per-slice regression testing matters, restated concretely here:
# baseline overall: 80% | candidate overall: 83% -- looks like a clear improvement
# baseline security slice: 85% | candidate security slice: 60% -- a SEVERE
# regression, completely hidden by the improved aggregate number -- exactly
# the kind of result a regression test must be designed to catch, not miss

lessons.title: Continuous Evaluation in Production
objectives: Design a continuous evaluation practice that closes the loop without treating noisy signals as ground truth
Explain how continuous evaluation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect continuous evaluation with delayed/unavailable labels and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Continuous evaluation means scheduled evaluation runs against the current system, safely sampling real production cases (with privacy considerations), human review queues for cases needing judgment, and dashboards tracking quality, latency, cost, and safety together over time.
examples:
# why user feedback alone is a limited, noisy signal for continuous evaluation:
# most users who had a fine experience never leave feedback at all
# users who DO leave feedback are not a representative sample of all users
# -- treating raw feedback volume/sentiment as ground truth risks reacting
# to a skewed, noisy signal rather than genuine system quality
commonMistakes: Treating raw user feedback or a single noisy production signal as definitive ground truth about system quality -- feedback is inherently unrepresentative and delayed, and reacting to it.
lessons.careerRelevance: This closing synthesis connects every earlier lesson into one continuous practice -- exactly the ongoing-responsibility mindset that distinguishes mature evaluation engineering from a one-time offline benchmark.

exercises.title: Convert a vague goal into measurable claims
exercises.prompt: Convert 'make the assistant better' into specific, testable evaluation claims.
exercises.hint: e.g. 'the assistant must never fabricate a specific dollar figure' (hard constraint) and 'it should correctly resolve at least 90% of billing questions without escalation' (optimization goal) -- specific and checkable, not vague

exercises.title: Choose the evaluation unit for a multi-turn assistant
exercises.prompt: A support assistant handles multi-turn conversations. What's the appropriate unit of evaluation, and why not just individual responses?
exercises.hint: the full conversation, since a single response might look fine in isolation while the overall conversation fails to resolve the user's actual issue

exercises.title: Choose offline, online, or combined evaluation
exercises.prompt: A team wants to know if a new prompt version improves customer satisfaction. Would offline evaluation alone answer this?
exercises.hint: not alone -- offline evaluation can check quality against a fixed dataset, but real customer satisfaction requires online evaluation (A/B testing, real user feedback) since offline and online evaluation answer different questions

exercises.title: Build a representative golden set
exercises.prompt: Design a golden dataset for a customer-support assistant, ensuring it's representative rather than just convenient.
exercises.hint: include a mix of real and synthetic cases across categories, difficulty levels, and user types -- not just the easy cases that happened to be readily available

exercises.title: Diagnose sampling bias in an easy-only set
exercises.prompt: An evaluation set contains only straightforward, easy examples. What's wrong, and what's the risk?
exercises.hint: sampling bias -- the set isn't representative of real difficulty distribution; a system can score very well on this set while failing badly on the harder, possibly more important cases it never gets tested against

exercises.title: Add adversarial and edge cases
exercises.prompt: An evaluation set only contains normal, everyday requests. Add adversarial and edge cases to it.
exercises.hint: e.g. deliberately ambiguous requests, unusually long inputs, requests designed to probe a known weak point, and requests from an edge-case user type not represented in the normal set

exercises.title: Identify a slice hidden by a strong aggregate score
exercises.prompt: A system shows 95% overall accuracy. What slice-level check would you run before trusting this number?
exercises.hint: break the score down by category, difficulty, and user type -- a 95% aggregate can hide a critical slice performing far worse, invisible in the single overall number

exercises.title: Choose metrics for a fixed task
exercises.prompt: A task requires the model to output valid JSON matching a schema. What metric type fits, and why not semantic similarity?
exercises.hint: schema/rule-based validation -- this is a deterministic, well-defined correctness question; semantic similarity is designed for open-ended meaning comparison, not structural validity checking

exercises.title: Design validation checks for model-generated JSON
exercises.prompt: Design the validation checks needed before model-generated JSON is used by a downstream system.
exercises.hint: valid JSON parsing, schema conformance, required fields present, correct types, enum/allowlist values, and range checks where applicable

exercises.title: Explain semantic similarity's factuality gap
exercises.prompt: Explain why a factually wrong answer can still score highly on semantic similarity to a correct reference.
exercises.hint: semantic similarity measures closeness in overall meaning and structure, not truth value -- a wrong number or fact stated in an otherwise similarly-structured sentence can still be very close in embedding space

exercises.title: Diagnose judge sensitivity
exercises.prompt: An automated judge's preference between two answers flips when their presentation order is swapped. What does this reveal, and what else might cause similar inconsistency?
exercises.hint: answer-order sensitivity -- a documented judge bias; verbosity preference (favoring longer answers) and rubric ambiguity can cause similar inconsistency

exercises.title: Design a counterbalanced pairwise protocol
exercises.prompt: Design a pairwise comparison protocol that avoids position bias.
exercises.hint: present candidate A first for half the comparisons and candidate B first for the other half, so any position bias present cancels out rather than contaminating the result

exercises.title: Write a human-evaluation rubric with scoring anchors
exercises.prompt: Write a rubric for rating response helpfulness on a 1-5 scale, including concrete scoring anchors.
exercises.hint: e.g. '5 = fully resolves the question with accurate, complete detail; 3 = partially helpful but missing key information; 1 = unhelpful or misleading' -- with a worked example at each anchor

exercises.title: Design a disagreement and adjudication policy
exercises.prompt: Two human reviewers disagree on a response's score. Design a policy for handling this.
exercises.hint: a defined adjudication process -- e.g. a third reviewer breaks ties, or disagreements above a certain gap are escalated to a senior reviewer -- rather than leaving disagreement unresolved or averaged blindly

exercises.title: Separate retrieval from generation failure
exercises.prompt: A RAG system gives a wrong answer. The retrieved document was actually correct and relevant. What's the failure category, and what should be fixed?
exercises.hint: generation failure -- the right context was retrieved, but the model still produced a wrong or ungrounded answer from it; the fix is in prompting/generation, not retrieval

exercises.title: Evaluate an agent's tool choice and side effects
exercises.prompt: An agent's final answer says a task completed successfully. What specific things would you check beyond that final text?
exercises.hint: tool selection (was the right tool used), argument correctness, sequence correctness, unnecessary tool calls, and actual side effects (what really changed in the system, not just what the agent claims)

exercises.title: Detect evaluation-set contamination
exercises.prompt: A model performs suspiciously well on a public benchmark compared to its performance on your own held-out cases. What might be happening?
exercises.hint: possible contamination -- the model may have seen the benchmark data during training (memorization rather than genuine generalization); your own held-out cases are a more trustworthy signal

exercises.title: Design a regression and continuous-evaluation plan
exercises.prompt: Design a plan balancing quality, latency, and cost for ongoing regression testing of a production LLM feature.
exercises.hint: a versioned golden dataset, per-slice thresholds (not just aggregate), a defined acceptable trade-off (e.g. how much latency increase is acceptable for a given quality gain), and scheduled continuous runs with alerting on regressions

quiz.q: What should evaluation begin with, according to this course's central principle?
options: Choosing a convenient, available metric
Defining what specific claim or property the system is supposed to satisfy
Picking the most popular benchmark
Running the largest possible test set

quiz.q: What is a genuine risk of evaluating only successful examples?
options: No real risk exists
It reveals nothing about where the system actually fails, since only cases it already handles well were tested
Success-only testing is always sufficient
Successful examples always generalize perfectly

quiz.q: Why can offline and online evaluation results genuinely differ?
options: They never differ in practice
Offline evaluation uses a fixed dataset, while online evaluation reflects real user behavior the fixed dataset may not fully capture
Online evaluation is always less accurate
Offline evaluation always predicts production performance exactly

quiz.q: What does canary evaluation conceptually provide that pure offline evaluation cannot?
options: Nothing additional
Real signal from production traffic, at controlled, limited exposure before full rollout
A replacement for all offline testing
Guaranteed immediate labels

quiz.q: Why must a golden dataset avoid reusing examples from development/prompt iteration?
options: Reuse is always fine
The system may have been implicitly tuned against those exact examples, inflating apparent performance without measuring real generalization
Development examples are always lower quality
This has no effect on evaluation results

quiz.q: What can an aggregate evaluation score hide?
options: Nothing, aggregate scores are always fully informative
A serious regression in a smaller but potentially critical slice of cases
Aggregate scores are never useful

quiz.q: When is exact-match a poor metric choice?
options: It's always the best choice for any task
For open-ended, free-form output where a valid paraphrase would incorrectly fail the check
Exact match never has any limitations
Only when evaluating JSON output

quiz.q: Do precision, recall, and F1 apply to every evaluation task?
options: Yes, universally
No -- only where the task has a genuine notion of correct/incorrect classification or retrieval
They apply only to open-ended generation tasks
These metrics are obsolete and should never be used

quiz.q: What are two documented failure modes of LLM-as-a-judge?
options: Judges have no known failure modes
Answer-order sensitivity and verbosity preference
Judges are always more reliable than deterministic metrics
Judges only fail when the underlying model is very small

quiz.q: Why should an automated judge's output be calibrated against human-reviewed examples?
options: Calibration is unnecessary if the judge produces a number
A judge is a measurement tool with documented biases, not an unquestionable authority, and calibration helps audit its reliability
Judges are always perfectly calibrated by default
Human review is never needed once a judge exists

quiz.q: Why is pairwise comparison often more reliable than absolute scoring?
options: It never is more reliable
Humans and judges are typically better at relative comparison than assigning a stable absolute number
Pairwise comparison requires no counterbalancing
Absolute scoring is always simpler and equally reliable

quiz.q: What does a well-designed human-evaluation rubric require beyond a numeric scale?
options: Nothing beyond a number is needed
Concrete scoring anchors with examples of what each score level actually looks like
Numeric scales are always sufficient on their own
Rubrics should avoid any concrete examples

quiz.q: How does faithfulness to provided context differ from factual correctness?
options: They are identical concepts
Faithfulness asks whether the response accurately reflects what was given, even if that source itself were wrong; factual correctness asks whether a claim is true in the world
Faithfulness is a stricter version of factual correctness
Factual correctness only applies to RAG systems

quiz.q: Can a response be fluent and relevant while still being factually unsupported?
options: No, fluency guarantees correctness
Yes -- fluency and relevance are properties of the text, not evidence of truth
Relevance always implies factual accuracy
This situation cannot occur in practice

quiz.q: Why must RAG evaluation separate retrieval performance from generation performance?
options: There's no reason to separate them
A bad answer can result from either failure, and each requires a different fix -- misattributing the cause means fixing the wrong part of the pipeline
Retrieval and generation always fail together
Generation failures are always more common than retrieval failures

quiz.q: What does context precision conceptually measure in RAG evaluation?
options: The total number of documents in the index
How much of what was actually retrieved was genuinely relevant to the query
The model's output token count
The speed of the retrieval step

quiz.q: Why must agent evaluation examine actions and tool effects, not just the final answer?
options: The final answer always reflects everything that happened
An agent can produce a reasonable-sounding final answer while having taken wrong or unauthorized actions along the way
Actions never diverge from what the final answer describes
Tool effects are irrelevant to evaluation

quiz.q: What does structured-output evaluation check that a subjective helpfulness rubric does not?
options: They check the exact same thing
Well-defined, deterministic correctness (schema, required fields, allowed values) rather than an open-ended quality judgment
Structured-output checks are always subjective too
Helpfulness rubrics are unnecessary once schema validation passes

quiz.q: Why is per-slice regression testing important, beyond checking the aggregate score?
options: Aggregate scores always reveal every regression
An aggregate improvement can hide a serious regression in a specific, possibly critical, slice
Per-slice testing is only relevant for RAG systems
Aggregate and per-slice results are always identical

quiz.q: What does evaluation-data contamination risk?
options: No real risk to evaluation validity
A model may have seen benchmark data during training, making results reflect memorization rather than genuine generalization
Contamination only affects human evaluation
Contamination always improves evaluation accuracy

interviewPreparation.q: How would you evaluate an LLM feature before releasing it?
interviewPreparation.a: Start by defining the specific claim the feature needs to satisfy, build a representative golden dataset with slices and edge/adversarial cases, select metrics appropriate to each claim (deterministic, semantic, or human/judge-based as fitting), and check offline results per-slice, not just in aggregate, before considering online evaluation.

interviewPreparation.q: What are the risks of using an LLM as the judge of another LLM?
interviewPreparation.a: Documented failure modes include answer-order sensitivity, verbosity preference, rubric ambiguity, and judge/model coupling with shared blind spots -- an automated judge is a measurement tool with these biases, not an unquestionable authority, and its output should be calibrated against human-reviewed examples.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you build a representative golden evaluation dataset?
interviewPreparation.a: Combine real and synthetic cases across categories, difficulty levels, and user-type slices, explicitly include adversarial and edge cases rather than only typical usage, document why each case is included, version the dataset, and avoid accidentally reusing development/prompt-iteration examples as evaluation cases.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you evaluate a RAG system and determine whether a bad answer came from retrieval or generation?
interviewPreparation.a: Separately check whether the relevant document was actually retrieved (a retrieval failure if not) versus whether the model produced a wrong or ungrounded answer despite having the right context available (a generation failure) -- the fix differs entirely depending on which stage actually failed.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you detect a regression after changing a prompt or model version?
interviewPreparation.a: Compare baseline and candidate results against a versioned evaluation dataset, checking both the overall score and per-slice scores -- since an improved aggregate can hide a regression in a specific, possibly critical slice -- and apply a predefined threshold for what counts as an acceptable trade-off versus a clear regression.

capstone.title: Design and Build a Production LLM Evaluation System
capstone.description: Given a realistic AI feature (customer-support assistant, internal knowledge assistant, document-analysis assistant, or tool-using workflow assistant), design and build a complete evaluation system covering every stage from goal definition through continuous production evaluation.
deliverables: Golden dataset with representative slices, normal, edge, and adversarial cases
Semantic or rubric-based evaluation where appropriate

At least 3 explicit trade-off explanations (e.g. evaluation coverage vs. review cost, automated grading vs. human reliability, quality vs. latency, quality vs. serving cost, strict thresholds vs. false alarms, production sampling vs. privacy)
One deliberately simplified or manual component, with justification
One metric the learner deliberately refuses to treat as sufficient on its own
One critical slice that must not be hidden by the aggregate score
One scenario where the correct conclusion is 'insufficient evidence'
capstone.portfolioTips: The required 'insufficient evidence' scenario and the refused-sufficient metric are what distinguish a genuine evaluation system from a checklist -- explicitly naming the limits of your own evaluation is exactly the honesty real evaluation engineering roles expect.

industryUsage.usage: All publish evaluation methodology distinguishing offline benchmarks from production monitoring, and documenting known LLM-as-judge biases -- directly reflecting this course's core principles.

industryUsage.company: Companies running production LLM features at scale
industryUsage.usage: Per-slice regression testing and continuous production evaluation, as covered in this course, are exactly what prevents a well-intentioned prompt or model update from silently shipping a regression.

careerApplications: Used by AI/ML engineers to define evaluation sets and metrics, compare model or prompt changes, detect regressions, analyze failures, and decide whether an LLM change is safe to ship.
